extracted.intended_audience: NIH extramural research community (investigators, grant applicants, institutional administrators, and reviewers)
extracted.subtask_description: Short news-style guidance and updates about NIH extramural policies and resources that affect preparing and submitting grant applications (e.g., model selection, data management plans, replication/reproducibility expectations, peer review outcomes). Aimed at helping applicants and institutions comply with current NIH expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting appropriate models (New Approach Methodologies - NAMs)
rubrics_metrics.description: “NIH supports a wide range of scientifically sound approaches to advance our understanding of human health and disease. As we continue to encourage approaches that enhance human relevance and translational potential, investigators should still select the models most appropriate for their specific research questions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose research models that best answer the scientific question; prioritize human relevance and translational potential where appropriate. NAMs are supported but selection must be justified by fit to the research question (no one-size-fits-all).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the 2026 Pilot Data Management and Sharing (DMS) Plan format
rubrics_metrics.description: “We have issued a new 2026 Pilot DMS Plan format based on a simplified set of required elements to use when preparing Data Management and Sharing (DMS) Plans.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare DMS plans using the 2026 pilot format and include the simplified set of required elements specified by NIH. Follow the prescribed format rather than ad hoc approaches to ensure compliance with current NIH expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embed replication and reproducibility throughout NIH research
rubrics_metrics.description: “The reliability of biomedical research is foundational to public trust in science and to ensuring that findings can benefit patients and communities. NIH’s Gold Standard Science plan advances this commitment by encouraging a culture that values replication and reproducibility. In support of this plan, NIH has launched a new Replication and Reproducibility Initiative to drive, incentivize and institutionalize replication and reproducibility efforts across the biomedical research enterprise.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design studies, analysis plans, and proposals to explicitly address replication and reproducibility (e.g., reproducible methods, transparent reporting, replication studies where appropriate). Expect initiatives and funding opportunities that incentivize and institutionalize replication/reproducibility practices; highlight how your project supports reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the 'Competitive But Not Discussed' review outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: “Recognizing that strong applications may fall below a 33% cut off, the middle third of applications in a study section were designated as ‘competitive but not discussed.’”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that an application scored in the middle third may be labeled 'competitive but not discussed' — a change from prior practice due to review modifications. This affects interpretation of review outcomes and subsequent steps (e.g., resubmission strategy, administrative follow-up).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use NIH-produced resources (overviews, videos, Data Book) to prepare applications
rubrics_metrics.description: References to resources such as a 6-minute overview video for the new Collaborative International Research Project (PF5) award structure and FY2025 updates in the NIH Data Book intended to help applicants learn key features and formats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult NIH videos, overviews, and the NIH Data Book to learn key award features, application formats, and administrative details (for example, how PF5 applications may be split into linked awards after review). Using official NIH resources helps ensure correct format and understanding of program specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for effects of centralized peer review (CSR consolidation)
rubrics_metrics.description: “In March 2025, NIH announced that all peer review would be centralized within the Center for Scientific Review (CSR) ... providing an update on the consolidation and its initial effects on the peer-review process.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that centralization of peer review may influence review timelines, study section composition, and emphasis on efficiency, competition, and transparency. Consider these changes when planning submission timing, application targeting, and response to review outcomes.
